audio_caption: The audio begins with a calm, welcoming voice introducing the focus of the presentation: cell membranes, also known as plasma membranes, lipid bilayers, or plasmalemma. The speaker, who sounds like a male, conveys a tone that is informative and instructional. He announces that he will explain what a cell membrane or plasma membrane is.

The clip begins with a male speaker emphasizing the importance of a topic, proposing to explore it. He explains how it separates the cell's interior from the external environment, functioning as a wall and selectively allowing passage of cargo. He draws a parallel to airport passport control, restricting entry to those with proper documents. The speaker continues discussing plasma membrane proteins, describing them as passport control officers, keeping out undesirable elements and removing waste. He further states that these transport nutrients into and expel waste from the cell, considering it a very important role.

The clip begins with a male speaker discussing different types of cell membranes, noting they will focus on a general model. He describes the plasma membrane's structure as interesting because it is both simple and complicated, and then states it's made up of lipids, proteins, and cholesterol, consisting largely of a phospholipid bilayer. He says that the outer layer is made of several components. Cholesterol, he clarifies, is present on both sides of the cell membrane. The speaker transitions to discussing membrane proteins.

The audio begins with a male speaker discussing the plasma membrane, its composition of lipids, proteins, and cholesterol. He clarifies a statement, mentioning lipids form the "fundamental part of this lipid bilayer," while proteins carry out membrane functions. He states the plasma membrane is approximately 50% protein and 50% lipid, with a carbohydrate portion of 5 to 10%.

The clip begins with a single male speaker describing how two scientists proposed "the fluid mosaic model of plasma membrane in 1972." He states that this is now "accepted as a basic model of all biological membrane." The speaker then asks, "What is about what is fluid mosaic model?" before summarizing that according to the model, "there are integral membrane proteins and peripheral proteins". The speaker sounds professional and educational.

The audio begins with a male speaker explaining the differences between integral and peripheral proteins, noting that integral proteins are embedded in the membrane, while peripheral proteins are indirectly bound. He continues to describe integral proteins as transmembrane proteins with portions exposed on both sides of the membrane, and glycosylated portions outside the membrane.

A male speaker, in an explanatory tone, describes "glycosylation", mentioning the attachment of carbohydrate moieties to hydroxyl groups. He points out "glycosylation right in the blue." He then suggests examining a phospholipid molecule in more detail.

The clip starts with a male speaker describing an interesting molecule, explaining it is both hydrophilic and hydrophobic, meaning it "loves and hates" water and referring to it as an amphiphilic molecule, comparing it to a "love and hate story with water." He then describes a phospholipid molecule and its head and tail. He then transitions to describing the phosphate group and molecule and moves on to describing saturated and unsaturated fatty acids. He then transitions again to talking about proteins.

A single, male speaker is describing integral proteins inside a membrane. He explains that some proteins are composed of multiple segments and are extensively folded. He uses an even, educational tone. The speaker describes the structures as alpha helix and better sheet. He then comments that these proteins are involved in cell signaling pathways and cargo transportation. The speaker compares their role to passport control officers. He mentions the cell membrane before transitioning to the topic of disease in plasma membrane.

The audio features a male speaker discussing the importance of the plasma membrane and the consequences of its integrity being disturbed. He mentions the composition of the membrane, "array of lipids and proteins," and the potential for "severe consequences" if damaged. The speaker's tone is informative and somewhat serious. The audio contains no identifiable music or background sounds.

The audio features a single male speaker discussing "diseases associated with disturbance in the membrane integrity", giving examples such as "high level of cholesterol in blood", diabetes, obesity, and Grave's disease, defining the latter as a disease of the immune system that "results in overproduction of thyroid hormones or so called as hyperthyroidism" with an informative and slightly technical tone.

A male speaker discusses cellular structure instability, mentioning its association with erythrocyte abnormalities and altered transport systems. He specifically references cystic fibrosis, a genetic disorder affecting mostly the lungs, but also other organs. He notes that the condition results from mutations in genes called cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, or CFTR. The speaker concludes that numerous diseases are associated with this mutation.

The clip begins with a male speaker emphasizing the importance of maintaining the "integrity of plasma membrane", noting that the cell does a good job at this.  He concludes the presentation, inviting questions and announcing the next topic will be cytoskeleton, sounding relaxed and informative.  He expresses gratitude for the listeners' time and invites them to subscribe for more "cell and molecular biology education and stuff", ending with a friendly farewell.
